narrative:
The model estimates that you have a 14% probability of failing your final year. That does not mean failure is certain, but in this review the estimate is being treated as a warning strong enough to require remedial courses.

The strongest influence in your profile was your record of past class failures. You have none, which matches the average among students who passed, so this worked in your favor and lowered the estimated risk. The next most important factor was the quality of your family relationships. You describe them as good, which is also the most common rating among students who passed, so this too pushed toward passing. Third was your reason for choosing the school: reputation. This is a common reason among passing students and also counted in your favor. In other words, the three most important factors did not drive the fail prediction; they all reduced the estimated risk. The final warning appears to come from the combined effect of other background and school-life factors rather than these top three.

To improve your position, keep your record free of failures, protect your attendance—your two absences are already below the passing average—and use the family support you have. Because your weekly study time is in the middle range, consider building a more consistent study routine and asking your guardian or school staff about structured remedial help. Treat the remedial courses as a chance to strengthen habits before the final assessments.
